targets.old_statement: Unposted rural roads cap at fifty-five while New York City defaults to twenty-five, and either limit still punishes unreasonable speed when fog or slick pavement demands less.
targets.old_spoken_statement: Unposted rural roads cap at fifty-five while New York City defaults to twenty-five, and either limit still punishes unreasonable speed when fog or slick pavement demands less.
targets.statement: Where no speed limit is posted, drive no faster than fifty-five miles per hour, whereas New York City defaults to twenty-five miles per hour unless another limit is posted, and even driving below a posted limit on a slippery or fogged road can draw a ticket for speed not reasonable for conditions.

targets.old_statement: The normal cushion counts two seconds but trucks and bad weather demand three or four, the only gap in the chapter that grows with conditions.
targets.old_spoken_statement: The normal cushion counts two seconds but trucks and bad weather demand three or four, the only gap in the chapter that grows with conditions.
targets.statement: Use the two-second rule for a normal following cushion, and increase that count to at least three or four seconds in bad weather or when following large trucks.

targets.old_statement: Entries yield everything leftward with the circle owning priority, the reverse of normal intersections where the newcomer often keeps going.
targets.old_spoken_statement: Entries yield everything leftward with the circle owning priority, the reverse of normal intersections where the newcomer often keeps going.
targets.statement: Drivers approaching a roundabout must yield at entry, look left because circulating traffic has the right-of-way, and wait for an adequate gap before entering.
